kurz: Which three functions money performs, how cash and account balances differ as two kinds of euro, and why today's money is backed by trust alone.

bloecke.md:
What money is follows from the functions it performs. A ten-euro note is printed cotton fibre, a balance in a current account is a line in a bank's database, a gold coin is a piece of metal. None of these objects is money in itself. They count as money only as long as other people accept them in exchange.

The material therefore does not tell you whether something is money. What matters is what an object has to do in order to serve as money.

## The three functions of money

As a **medium of exchange**, money removes the need for the double coincidence of wants that all trade without money requires. In direct barter, the baker has to need shoes, and at exactly the moment when the shoemaker wants bread. Money splits this unlikely exchange into two transactions, each of which is easy to arrange. This makes money convenient, and it also determines how far the division of labour can develop.

As a **unit of account**, money provides the yardstick in which all prices are expressed. Without this yardstick, every good would have to be valued against every other good. With *n* tradable goods, that means *n*×(*n*−1)/2 exchange ratios, so with 1,000 goods, 499,500 figures that nobody can know. With a unit of account, 1,000 prices are enough.

The third function is the **store of value**. Money carries purchasing power into the future, for example when someone sells their labour today and buys a flat in twenty years' time. This function is the most demanding of the three, and it is the only one that modern currencies deliberately fulfil only in part.

bloecke.md: An object is money if it performs all three functions at the same time. If one of them is missing, it is something else, such as an investment asset, a collector's item or a voucher. Most arguments about whether a particular thing is money can be settled by checking the three functions one by one.

## Properties of usable money

The three functions give rise to properties that have prevailed again and again throughout history. Usable money is:

- durable, because otherwise the stored value spoils along with the good
- divisible and able to be put back together, so that small amounts are possible too
- homogeneous, meaning every unit is the same as every other, because otherwise each piece has to be checked individually
- portable, meaning high in value and low in weight
- scarce, but not too scarce
- hard to counterfeit
- generally accepted; this is the only one of these properties that does not lie in the material, as it depends on what others think of it

In post-war Germany, the Reichsmark was nominally valid but practically worthless. Prices were frozen by the state, and goods were only available with ration coupons or on the black market. The American cigarette took the place of the Reichsmark. It was durable, homogeneous, easily divisible, easy to transport and scarce, and so had all the properties that textbooks attribute to commodity money.

Its only flaw was that it could be smoked. The money stock therefore shrank through consumption. For this reason the cigarette currency remained a stopgap. It disappeared within a few days in 1948, when there was once again money that people trusted.

## From commodity money to book money

Over the course of history, money has become ever more abstract. It starts with commodity money such as cattle, salt, shells or metal bars, whose value lies in the material. With minted coins, the stamp certifies weight and fineness, so that not every single trade needs a weighing any more. Paper money begins as a receipt. Anyone who deposits metal with a custodian receives a note promising to hand it back, and over time the note is passed on instead of the metal.

The most important step came in the 20th century, when convertibility into metal was abandoned bit by bit. It finally ended worldwide in 1971 with the end of the dollar's link to gold (see the separate lesson on this). Since then, money has been [[fiat money]], backed only by the expectation that it can be spent again tomorrow. Over the same period, by far the larger part of money shifted to accounts at banks.

ereignisse.text: Minted electrum coins appear in Lydia. The stamp replaces weighing and testing in every trade.
Under the Song dynasty, state-issued paper notes circulate for the first time.
Stockholms Banco issues the first European banknotes. It soon puts more notes into circulation than it can back.
On 15 November the Rentenmark is introduced, and from 20 November the ratio of 1 to 1 trillion paper marks applies. The depreciation of the currency ends almost immediately.

The Deutsche Mark is introduced on 20/21 June. Every person receives a per-capita allowance of DM 40, wages and rents are converted at 1:1, savings effectively at RM 100 to DM 6.50. The shop windows fill up immediately.
The USA suspends the convertibility of the dollar into gold at $35 per fine ounce. The other countries follow, and since then all money has been fiat money.
The euro starts as book money, and cash follows only three years later. The order shows that most money is book money.
A digital euro as direct central bank money for private individuals is in preparation but not yet introduced.

bloecke.md:
## Composition of the money supply

Most people think of cash when they think of money, yet cash makes up only a small part of the money supply. The broad money supply M3 of the euro area stood at €17,614 billion in July 2026. Of this, €1,613 billion was cash, around 9%. The largest block was overnight deposits at €9,680 billion, that is, ordinary balances in current accounts and instant-access savings accounts.

Together with time and savings deposits, around 84% of money is [[book money]]. Book money is a claim on a private commercial bank and is created as the counter-entry to that bank's loans. The next lesson covers how this works in detail.

bloecke.titel: Central bank money and book money
bloecke.md:
[[Central bank money]] and commercial bank money bear the same name but are legally different things. Cash is a direct claim on the central bank and the only central bank money that private individuals can hold. The balance in your account is a claim on a private bank, protected by the statutory deposit protection of €100,000 per customer and institution.

In everyday life the difference goes unnoticed, because banks exchange balances for cash at any time. In a banking crisis, on the other hand, it is what matters most. This gap is the main argument for a digital euro.

## Trust as backing

The term “legal tender” only means that nobody may refuse to accept it in settlement of a debt. It says nothing about the value of the money. Money has value as long as the issuing body credibly ensures that the quantity issued remains scarce.

German history provides two pieces of evidence for this, in both directions. In 1923 the exchange rate rose from 4.20 marks per dollar (July 1914) to around 4.2 trillion marks per dollar (20 November 1923), that is, by a factor of one trillion. The Rentenmark had been introduced five days earlier. At this rate, the ratio of 1 Rentenmark to 1 trillion marks applied, and inflation ended practically at once. Formally, the Rentenmark was backed by a land charge (Grundschuld) on the landed property of agriculture, industry and commerce, but it could not be redeemed in gold. Its value was secured above all by a credible self-commitment to strictly limit the quantity in circulation. In 1948 the same sequence was repeated, when the black market disappeared within days of the introduction of the Deutsche Mark. Both times, savers lost out. In 1948 balances were effectively converted at a ratio of 100 Reichsmarks to 6.50 Deutsche Marks, while wages and rents stayed at 1 to 1.

The statement “bad money drives out good” only holds if an officially fixed rate sets both kinds at the same face value. If someone then owns a full-weight and a worn silver coin, they spend the worn one and keep the good one. The good money disappears from circulation because it is undervalued at the fixed rate.

Without a legally enforced rate, the statement is reversed. When rates are set freely, the better money prevails, which is known in the literature as Thiers' law. One piece of evidence for this is the cigarette currency of 1945. The Reichsmark was compulsory legal tender and was nevertheless shunned, because its face value no longer had anything to do with its worth.

## Store of value as the weakest function

As a medium of exchange and a unit of account, the euro works flawlessly. As a store of value it has gaps by design, because monetary policy does not aim for constant prices. Its goal is a small, steady loss of purchasing power.

This loss can be measured. The German consumer price index stood at 125.8 points in August 2026 (2020 = 100). A basket of goods that cost €100 in 2020 therefore costs around €126 today. Conversely, a €100 note put aside in 2020 now buys goods worth only around €79.50. In six years, around a fifth of purchasing power has thus been lost without anyone debiting anything.

Interest does not automatically make up for this loss. The ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026, and German inflation was 2.9% in August 2026. If €10,000 is invested at this rate, there is €10,250 in the account after one year. This buys goods that cost around €9,960 today. So the balance has grown in nominal terms, while in real terms it has lost purchasing power.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of the purchasing power of an amount put aside today, assuming constant inflation. Even at the target of 2%, it halves in just over 35 years.

bloecke.md: It makes sense to separate the two jobs your own money is supposed to do. Money needed as a means of payment and as a reserve belongs in an account. There, the loss of purchasing power costs little, because the amount is small and the period short. Money that is meant to preserve purchasing power over decades is poorly placed in a currency whose issuer explicitly aims for 2% depreciation a year.

mitnehmen: Money is defined by its three functions (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value) and not by its material.
Around 84% of money in the euro area is book money, that is, claims on private banks and not on the central bank.

Since 1971 no major currency has been backed by a commodity any more; the value of each rests solely on the credibility of its issuer. The years 1923 and 1948 show that this is enough, and that savers bear the cost.
Store of value is the weakest function, because a consumer price index of 125.8 means around a fifth less purchasing power since 2020.
Gresham's law only applies under a legally enforced rate; when rates are set freely, the better money prevails.

begriffe.text: Money with no claim to redemption in a commodity. Its value rests solely on general acceptance and on the scarcity policy of the issuing central bank. Since 1971 this has applied to all major currencies.
Balances in accounts at commercial banks, also called deposit money. Legally a claim on the bank, not on the central bank. In the euro area, around 84% of the money supply M3.
Money created by the central bank, that is, cash and banks' balances at the central bank. So far, private individuals can only hold it in the form of cash.
The function of money as a common measure of value. It reduces the number of price quotations needed from n×(n−1)/2 exchange ratios to n prices.
With an officially fixed exchange rate, the worse money drives the better money out of circulation, because the better money is hoarded. Without a legally enforced rate, the effect is reversed.
A means of payment that may not be refused in settlement of a monetary debt. The term concerns the obligation to accept it and says nothing about its value.
